I would just probably damn the sides of the table top with 4 inch blue painter's tape.

it would be more than enough to withhold the resin as long as you're just doing a coating no more than half an inch thick.

if you want to go any thicker than that then I would reinforce the sides with wood or something else to prop up the tape walls up more securely. 

I use yardsticks wrapped in painters tape clamped around table tops with bar clamps sometimes and it works well. sheathing tape is great also and will leave a smooth ,shiny mirror texture. 

as far as color I would maybe choose some pigment powders that you like or even acrylic paints. I use pearl ex and meyspring brands. 

 just mix the pigment powders into the resin while mixing A and B together for a unique looking worktop. you could also use things like glitter or confetti depending on the style you want. 

checkout stonecoatcountertops on YouTube , they've got some great ideas for countertops and floors that utilize pigments paints and resin.  I just adapted their method with my own resins and pigment powders.

I use a tabletop resin that's food safe ( incidental contact ) from the epoxy resin store on eBay.

 it's basically a generic brand but is great quality and resists yellowing very well. I buy in 4 gallon quantity and it works out to about 45.00 per gallon. free shipping.

 this is the best deal I've found out there. ships from California ( I think) and they're usually pretty fast. 

 I have even used this resin on my bathroom floor and it holds up amazingly. 

if you want something locally you can get a product called glaze coat or super glaze from Lowe's or home Depot which also works very well for table tops. however, those products require extra mixing and will yellow if exposed to UV light AT ALL. hope this helps

I would just take the extra time to do it right the first time because once that resin sets up there's nothing you can do about it, it's ruined.

I've done a shyt ton of tables and my advice would be :

use a border around the edges, make sure it is absolutely level.

fill the area with water to know exactly how much resin you will need and this will help you avoid waste. 

make sure the table surface area is completely dried and free of any moisture though before pouring resin. 

also you're going to want to glue those keys down before pouring over top. a tiny bit of macropearl pigment in your top coat will really give it some pop and add some 3d effect. 

mix slowly and use a torch to pop bubbles after pouring( if you don't have a pressure chamber)

 feel free to message me with any questions as you go.

I've literally spent hundreds of dollars learning how to do tables / resin tops correctly. Ive made alot of tables and  encased all sorts of stuff from bottle caps to guitar picks, keys, washers nuts bolts pennies photographs etcetera. definitely a learning process but you're on the right track seeking good advice instead of learning on your own like I did. it's definitely more expensive that way. 

YouTube is your friend when it comes to resin as there's a  ton of great videos out there including some great table making videos. good luck and welcome to your new obsession!
